Scenario 01

Requests about your vehicle

2 cards

A calm response

“Officer, I’ll turn off the engine. I’d prefer to keep my keys with me. Is that a lawful order?”

If ordered out of the car, comply calmly. Do not physically resist or argue roadside. You can say: “I do not consent to any searches. I am exercising my right to remain silent.”

Keep in mind

  • Keep your hands visible.
  • Move slowly and narrate movements.
  • Ask whether it is a request or an order.
  • Never physically resist, even if you believe an order is unlawful.
⚖

Legal context

What the cited cases actually establish

During a lawful traffic stop, an officer may order a driver out of the vehicle. A frisk requires reasonable suspicion that the person is armed and dangerous. The stop may not be prolonged beyond its traffic mission without independent reasonable suspicion. These decisions do not create a universal rule specifically governing every request for car keys; state law and the circumstances can matter.

Pennsylvania v. Mimms434 U.S. 106, 111 (1977) Arizona v. Johnson555 U.S. 323, 327 (2009) Rodriguez v. United States575 U.S. 348, 354–57 (2015)

A calm response

“Officer, I’ve provided my license, registration, and insurance. I choose not to answer other questions. Am I free to leave?”

If the officer presses, repeat calmly: “I’m not trying to be difficult. I choose not to answer questions. Am I free to go?” Asking does not end the stop—do not drive away until the officer clearly says you may leave.

Keep in mind

  • Provide documents required by your state’s law.
  • Do not lie or offer a made-up destination.
  • Keep your tone neutral and your hands visible.
  • Repeat the same short response instead of debating.
⚖

Legal context

Questions are allowed; added detention is limited

Officers may ask questions unrelated to the traffic violation while a lawful stop is underway, provided the questions do not measurably extend it. A routine roadside stop is generally not “custody” requiring Miranda warnings, though statements can still be used as evidence. Without independent reasonable suspicion, police may not add time to the stop to pursue unrelated investigation. Document and identification duties vary by state.

Berkemer v. McCarty468 U.S. 420, 435–42 (1984) Arizona v. Johnson555 U.S. 323, 333 (2009) Rodriguez v. United States575 U.S. 348, 354–57 (2015)
